OpenStax 12.3: Persuasion is the process of changing our attitude toward something based on some kind of communication.

Petty, Cacioppo and Goldman 1981: two basic routes to persuasion, one based on the thoughtful consideration of arguments central to the issue, the other on peripheral cues; OpenStax 12.3 gives attractiveness and celebrity-type cues for the peripheral route.

OpenStax 12.3: the central route, if successful, will result in lasting attitude change and works best when the audience is analytical and willing to process; the peripheral route typically results in less permanent attitude or behavior change.

Petty, Cacioppo and Goldman 1981 (University of Missouri): strong or weak arguments for a comprehensive exam; source a local high school class or the Carnegie Commission on Higher Education chaired by a Princeton professor; changes the following year or in 10 years.
Petty, Cacioppo and Goldman 1981 abstract: under high relevance, attitudes were influenced primarily by the quality of the arguments; under low relevance, primarily by the expertise of the source.
OpenStax 12.5: an in-group is a group that we identify with; an out-group is a group we view as fundamentally different from us; in-group bias: a preference for our own group over other groups.
OpenStax 12.5: These groups provide a powerful source of our identity and self-esteem (Tajfel and Turner, 1979).

Tajfel 1970 (Scientific American): at the University of Bristol, 64 boys 14 and 15 years old; in a later experiment preferences for paintings by Paul Klee or Wassily Kandinsky; subjects were in fact assigned to groups at random.
Tajfel 1970: points were real money; awards were made to persons identified only by number and group; choices concerned members other than himself.
Tajfel 1970: a large majority of the subjects gave more money to members of their own group; at the sacrifice of utilitarian advantages, maximization of difference seemed more important to them.

Tajfel 1970: discrimination can be expected even if the individual is not involved in conflicts of interest and has no past history of hostility; it was enough for them to see themselves categorized into an ingroup and an outgroup.
